models.approach: Trace the rise to the disappearance of predictable adulthood, then follow the consequences into work and health systems.
plan: Introduction: name the trend and promise causes then consequences.
Body 1: causes, ranked, with economic insecurity first.
Body 2: consequences, joined explicitly to those causes.

paras.text: Anxiety and depression among people in their twenties have risen faster than in any other age group, and the increase is too steep to be explained by better diagnosis alone. [[It is evident that]] something in the conditions of young adulthood has changed, and the consequences are already visible in workplaces and clinics.

[[The main point is]] the loss of a predictable path. Previous generations could expect secure work and eventually a home; a graduate today may hold six short contracts before thirty, and [[in the long run]] that uncertainty is more corrosive than hardship itself, because it removes any ability to plan. Social media [[exacerbates|Exacerbate]] it by supplying constant comparison at exactly the age when comparison bites hardest. [[At the same time]], the informal networks that once absorbed distress, extended family, church, union, have thinned, leaving the individual to carry it alone.

[[As a result]], the effects reach well beyond the individual. Health systems designed for physical illness are [[inundated|Inundate]] by demand they cannot meet, and waiting lists of a year are now ordinary. Employers report absence and turnover concentrated among their youngest staff, which is expensive and largely invisible in the accounts. [[It follows that]] a generation entering work with untreated illness will carry the cost of it for decades.

[[In conclusion]], the rise is driven mainly by insecurity rather than by fragility, which is encouraging in one respect: causes of that kind are policy, not fate. Stable contracts, affordable housing and treatment available within weeks rather than years would [[ameliorate]] a problem that is otherwise certain to grow.

notes: Ranking the causes and saying which is primary is what the question is testing. Three equal causes read as a list rather than an analysis.
Untreated illness carried for decades is a consequence with a timescale, which is more useful than saying it is bad for society.
Policy, not fate is the essay's argument in three words, and it earns its place because the causes named were all structural.

models.stance: Attention and comparison as the cause
models.approach: Argue that the sharpest change is in the daily texture of attention rather than in economics.
plan: Introduction: the timing points at something more specific than the economy.
Body 1: causes, the phone, sleep and constant comparison.
Body 2: consequences for education, relationships and health services.
Conclusion: what could be changed, and what probably cannot.

paras.text: Economic explanations for rising anxiety are plausible but they fit the timing badly, since the sharpest increase began around 2012 rather than in the crash of 2008. [[I would argue]] that the more [[compelling]] cause is a change in how young adults spend their attention.

[[First and foremost]], sleep has been displaced. A phone beside the bed removes an hour or more a night, and disrupted sleep is one of the few [[empirical]] predictors of depression that nobody disputes. [[This leads to]] the second cause: continuous comparison. Where earlier generations compared themselves with thirty classmates, a nineteen-year-old now compares an ordinary Tuesday with the edited highlights of thousands of strangers, and the resulting sense of falling short is [[insidious]] rather than dramatic. [[Not surprisingly]], the effect is strongest among young women.

[[As a result]], the damage shows first where concentration is required. Universities report sharp rises in withdrawal and in requests for extensions, and employers find that new graduates need far more support than a decade ago. Friendships suffer too, since a conversation conducted in text is thinner than one conducted in a room, and thin friendships are poor protection. [[Consequently]], demand for treatment has grown faster than any health service can [[implement]] capacity.

[[Overall]], the causes lie in the ordinary daily habits of a generation, which is both hopeful and difficult. Phones out of bedrooms and out of schools would help, and [[to some degree]] the culture is already turning, but a technology this [[ingrained]] will not be legislated away.

notes: Using the timing to reject the alternative explanation is a strong opening move, and it costs one sentence.
Sleep is the mechanism that makes this essay concrete. A cause with a physiological pathway is more convincing than a cause described as a mood.
The conclusion admits the limits of its own remedy, which reads as honesty rather than weakness.

models.approach: Accept that the causes are multiple and argue that what unites them is the loss of predictable belonging.
plan: Introduction: single-cause explanations all fail; name the thread.
Body 1: three causes and the thread that joins them.
Body 2: consequences at the level of the person and of society.

paras.text: Every single-cause explanation for this rise fails a simple test: the trend appears in countries with very different economies and very different phone habits. [[From my perspective]] the causes are multiple, and what they share is the removal of predictable belonging.

[[The key issue is]] that three separate supports weakened at once. Work became [[intermittent]], so identity could no longer rest on a job; local institutions emptied, so it could not rest on a place; and friendship migrated onto platforms that measure it, so it could not rest on people either. Each alone would be manageable. Together they leave a young adult with no [[intact]] structure to fall back on, and the resulting [[introspection]] turns inward on the self as the only remaining subject.

[[As a result]], distress that would once have been absorbed privately now arrives as clinical demand. Services built for a smaller caseload are overwhelmed, and the wait itself worsens the illness. [[Broadly speaking]], a cohort that postpones work, partnership and children is not merely unhappy; it changes the shape of the population, and the economic consequences of that will outlast the psychological ones.

[[To sum up]], the increase reflects the simultaneous loss of several ordinary certainties rather than any single villain. [[It stands to reason]] that the response must be equally broad: secure work, funded local institutions and early treatment, since restoring any one of the three alone would leave the other two doing the damage.

notes: Rejecting single-cause explanations and then naming what unites several is the most sophisticated shape this question allows.
Three supports, named in one sentence each, keeps a multi-cause paragraph from turning into a list.
The conclusion insists that partial remedies fail, which follows directly from the argument rather than being added at the end.
